bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 8: Analyzing Sentence Structure
bib.venue: O'Reilly Media (book chapter; year inferred from the O'Reilly NLTK book, not printed in the chapter text)

question: How can the structure of arbitrarily many sentences be described with a finite grammar, and how can parsers recover that structure and cope with ambiguity?
contributions: Motivates grammars from structural (attachment) ambiguity and recursion, using the 'I shot an elephant in my pajamas' example
Defines context-free grammars, constituents and treebank-derived productions, and walks through recursive descent, shift-reduce, left-corner and chart (well-formed substring table) parsers
Introduces dependency grammar, projectivity, subcategorization, treebank searching, the growth of parse counts and probabilistic CFGs (PCFG) with Viterbi parsing

results.claim: The number of parses of a sentence with ambiguous attachment grows with the Catalan numbers: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ... up to 208,012 for length 23, the average WSJ Penn Treebank sentence length.
results.setup: 'fish fish fish...' sentences of length 3, 5, 7, ...; the last value corresponds to length 23
results.note: Church and Patil (1982) show PP attachment ambiguity grows in proportion to the Catalan numbers.

results.claim: For a sentence of length 50 there would be over 10^12 parses.
results.setup: Same Catalan growth; text prints '1012' for 10 to the power 12 after extraction
results.note: Superscript lost in extraction; the book means 10^12.

results.claim: A PCFG assigns a parse the product of its production probabilities; the sample grammar parses 'Jack saw telescopes' with p=0.064.
PCFG productions with the same left-hand side must have probabilities that sum to one (VP: 0.4+0.3+0.3).
A recursive descent parser loops forever on left-recursive productions such as NP -> NP PP, wastes time on structures that do not match the input, and rebuilds discarded subtrees after backtracking.
results.quote:
left-recursive productions
like NP -> NP PP send it into an infinite loop

results.claim: The WFST used as a toy chart parser only recognizes a sentence, requires binary rules, is wasteful bottom-up, and overwrote the second of two VP readings in cell (2,8).
results.setup: Section 8.4, complete_wfst on the 'I shot an elephant in my pajamas' grammar
results.quote:
the WFST is not itself a parse
tree

results.claim: The Penn Treebank sample in NLTK is a 10% sample, searchable to learn grammar facts such as which verbs take sentential complements.
results.setup: nltk.corpus.treebank, 10% sample of the Penn Treebank Corpus

limits: No parser is scored on accuracy or speed; the chapter is a conceptual and code walkthrough, and the grammars are toy-sized.
Probabilistic parsing is introduced with one hand-written PCFG; no induction of PCFG probabilities from a treebank is shown or evaluated.
Code uses Python 2 and NLTK 2 APIs (print statement, nbest_parse, .node).
The chapter predates neural dependency and constituency parsers, so it says nothing about how modern parsers rank parses.
practices: Write a grammar to describe constituent structure only after identifying the head and its complements, and test substitution of word sequences to find constituents (8.1, 8.2).
Prefer chart parsing (dynamic programming) over backtracking recursive descent for anything but demos, since it stores intermediate constituents and avoids infinite left-recursion loops (8.4).
Use a treebank to look up the grammar the data actually uses, such as verbs that take S complements, before writing productions (8.6).
Rank candidate parses with a weighted or probabilistic grammar rather than enumerate all, since the count grows with the Catalan numbers (8.6).
Use dependency grammar when you want grammatical functions (subject, object) directly, and check whether the graph is projective (8.5).

terms.definition: a group of words that behaves as a single unit and can be substituted for another unit of the same category
a set of productions A -> alpha with one non-terminal on the left
a sentence with more than one syntactic analysis, such as prepositional phrase attachment
a grammar relating each word to a head by labelled arcs instead of building phrases
a dependency graph whose arcs can be drawn above the words without crossing
a context-free grammar whose productions carry probabilities, summing to one per left-hand side
